results.name: odd_mult3_set_nonmult3_vs_mult3
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all odd multiples of 3 (e.g. 69,9,39,21; 63,27,99,33), yes rate for non-example odd targets that are NOT multiples of 3 minus non-example multiples of 3; observed above null means people read such sets as "odd" (or digit patterns) rather than "multiples of 3" more than the model, below means they favour "multiples of 3" more.
results.code:
# name: odd_mult3_set_nonmult3_vs_mult3
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all odd multiples of 3 (e.g. 69,9,39,21; 63,27,99,33), yes rate for non-example odd targets that are NOT multiples of 3 minus non-example multiples of 3; observed above null means people read such sets as "odd" (or digit patterns) rather than "multiples of 3" more than the model, below means they favour "multiples of 3" more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    P = set(n for n in range(2, 101) if all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)))
    def m(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    e = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=3.0)
    sel = (k >= 2) & (e % 2 == 1).all(1) & (e % 3 == 0).all(1) & ~is_ex
    return m(sel & (t % 2 == 1) & (t % 3 != 0)) - m(sel & (t % 3 == 0))

results.name: single_example_distance_corr
results.description: Among single-example sets, Pearson correlation between yes and |target - example| for non-example targets; observed more negative than null means people's yes rate falls off with numeric distance more steeply than the model, less negative means the model's distance gradient is too steep.
results.code:
# name: single_example_distance_corr
# description: Among single-example sets, Pearson correlation between yes and |target - example| for non-example targets; observed more negative than null means people's yes rate falls off with numeric distance more steeply than the model, less negative means the model's distance gradient is too steep.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    P = set(n for n in range(2, 101) if all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)))
    def m(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    sel = (k == 1) & ~is_ex
    if sel.sum() < 3:
        return 0.0
    dd = np.abs(t[sel] - ex[sel, 0]); yy = y[sel]
    if dd.std() == 0 or yy.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(dd, yy)[0, 1])

results.name: shared_digit_nonfinal_set_contains_lift
results.description: Among sets of 3+ examples that all contain a common digit d but do not all end in d (e.g. 83,38,58,68), yes rate for non-example targets containing d minus targets not containing d; observed above null means people generalise "contains d" more than the model, below means less.
results.code:
# name: shared_digit_nonfinal_set_contains_lift
# description: Among sets of 3+ examples that all contain a common digit d but do not all end in d (e.g. 83,38,58,68), yes rate for non-example targets containing d minus targets not containing d; observed above null means people generalise "contains d" more than the model, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    P = set(n for n in range(2, 101) if all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)))
    def m(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    e = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=-1).astype(int)
    tt = t.astype(int)
    lift_num = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool); sel_any = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    out = []
    for d in range(10):
        has = ((e % 10 == d) | ((e // 10) % 10 == d) & (e >= 10) | (e == 100) & (d in (0, 1)))
        has = has | (e < 0)
        ends = (e % 10 == d) | (e < 0)
        s = (k >= 3) & has.all(1) & ~ends.all(1) & ~is_ex
        tc = (tt % 10 == d) | (((tt // 10) % 10 == d) & (tt >= 10)) | ((tt == 100) & (d in (0, 1)))
        sel_any |= s
        lift_num |= s & tc
    return m(lift_num) - m(sel_any & ~lift_num)

results.name: between_set_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across sets (with 20+ non-example trials) of the per-set yes rate on non-example targets; observed above null means sets differ in overall generalisation more than the model predicts (model too homogeneous), below means less.
results.code:
# name: between_set_yes_rate_sd
# description: Standard deviation across sets (with 20+ non-example trials) of the per-set yes rate on non-example targets; observed above null means sets differ in overall generalisation more than the model predicts (model too homogeneous), below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    P = set(n for n in range(2, 101) if all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)))
    def m(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    d = pd.DataFrame({"s": df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy(), "y": y})[~is_ex]
    g = d.groupby("s")["y"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    g = g[g["size"] >= 20]
    return float(g["mean"].std()) if len(g) > 1 else 0.0

results.name: shared_last_digit_set_mismatch_yes
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all share the same final digit (e.g. 97,77,87,47; 7,67; 81,71,21,31), yes rate for targets with a different final digit; observed below null means people reject off-rule targets more completely than the model (model's lapse/range fallback too generous), above means they accept them more.
results.code:
# name: shared_last_digit_set_mismatch_yes
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all share the same final digit (e.g. 97,77,87,47; 7,67; 81,71,21,31), yes rate for targets with a different final digit; observed below null means people reject off-rule targets more completely than the model (model's lapse/range fallback too generous), above means they accept them more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    P = set(n for n in range(2, 101) if all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)))
    def m(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    e = np.where(np.isnan(ex), ex[:, :1], ex)
    same = (e % 10 == (e[:, :1] % 10)).all(1)
    sel = (k >= 2) & same & (t % 10 != e[:, 0] % 10)
    return m(sel)

results.name: odd_composite_set_odd_vs_even_lift
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all odd and include at least one odd composite (not all prime), yes rate for non-example odd targets minus non-example even targets; observed above null means people extend "odd numbers" more than the model (prime-over-odd penalty too strong), below means less.
results.code:
# name: odd_composite_set_odd_vs_even_lift
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all odd and include at least one odd composite (not all prime), yes rate for non-example odd targets minus non-example even targets; observed above null means people extend "odd numbers" more than the model (prime-over-odd penalty too strong), below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    P = set(n for n in range(2, 101) if all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)))
    def m(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    e = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=1.0)
    comp = np.isin(ex, [n for n in range(4, 101) if n not in P])
    sel = (k >= 2) & (e % 2 == 1).all(1) & comp.any(1) & ~is_ex
    return m(sel & (t % 2 == 1)) - m(sel & (t % 2 == 0))

results.name: even_set_near_minus_far_even_target
results.description: Among sets of 2+ all-even examples, yes rate for non-example even targets within 5 of some example minus even targets 15+ away from every example; observed above null means people show a numeric-similarity gradient inside the rule stronger than the model, below means weaker.
results.code:
# name: even_set_near_minus_far_even_target
# description: Among sets of 2+ all-even examples, yes rate for non-example even targets within 5 of some example minus even targets 15+ away from every example; observed above null means people show a numeric-similarity gradient inside the rule stronger than the model, below means weaker.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    P = set(n for n in range(2, 101) if all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)))
    def m(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    e = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=2.0)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), 1)
    sel = (k >= 2) & (e % 2 == 0).all(1) & ~is_ex & (t % 2 == 0)
    return m(sel & (dist <= 5)) - m(sel & (dist >= 15))

results.name: power_set_inrange_nonpower_yes
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all perfect powers (squares, cubes, powers of 2, incl. 1), yes rate for non-example targets that are not perfect powers and lie within the examples' [min,max]; observed above null means people fall back on a numeric range after power sets more than the model, below means less.
results.code:
# name: power_set_inrange_nonpower_yes
# description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all perfect powers (squares, cubes, powers of 2, incl. 1), yes rate for non-example targets that are not perfect powers and lie within the examples' [min,max]; observed above null means people fall back on a numeric range after power sets more than the model, below means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    k = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    is_ex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    P = set(n for n in range(2, 101) if all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)))
    def m(mask):
        return float(y[mask].mean()) if mask.sum() > 0 else 0.0
    pw = sorted(set([b ** e_ for b in range(1, 11) for e_ in range(2, 8) if b ** e_ <= 100] + [1]))
    isp = np.isin(ex, pw) | np.isnan(ex)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, 1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, 1)
    sel = (k >= 2) & isp.all(1) & ~is_ex & ~np.isin(t, pw) & (t >= lo) & (t <= hi)
    return m(sel)
